documents.title: PBAC Pharmaceutical Benefits Advisory Committee Australia

chunks.content: Key Points for Decision Makers Introduction Health technology assessment (HTA) is widely used to evaluate medicines in terms of their value for money and determine those that should be funded, particularly in the current climate of increased spending on healthcare and limited resources. HTA provides policymakers with a comprehensive approach to assessing a medicine's clinical effectiveness, safety, quality, and cost-effectiveness. Therefore, economic evaluation is considered the “fourth hurdle” for funding medicine [ ]. Economic models are often developed to synthesise evidence from clinical trials and other sources (e.g., literature, databases, surveys) to estimate the incremental cost-effectiveness ratio (ICER) of the proposed medicine compared to existing treatments. Medicines with ICERs that meet or lie below an explicitly or implicitly pre-specified ICER threshold are typically funded [ ]. However, when making recommendations, policymakers do not solely rely on the most likely ICER value but also systematically assess the uncertainties associated with it [ , ]. Such uncertainties are commonly encountered in economic models and may cause medicines to be rejected for funding, thus delaying patients' access to medicines. The systematic identification of uncertainties can help inform recommendations [ , ]. While some uncertainties are inherent in the treatment or disease and thus cannot be mitigated in the short term, other uncertainties may be reduced with alternative evidence or the collection of additional data. The value of information theory suggests that HTA bodies should prioritise mitigating those uncertainties when the cost of acquiring additional data is worthwhile [ ]. The ability to quantify the trade-off between the costs and benefits of obtaining additional data critically depends on how well the uncertainties have been characterised [ – ]. The first step in managing uncertainty in HTA is therefore to formally characterise the uncertainties involved [ ]. Generally, uncertainties in economic models can be categorised into four types: methodological, generalisability, structural, and parameter uncertainty [ , – ]. Methodological uncertainty occurs when the methods used deviate from the reference methodology suggested by the HTA guidelines [ , , , ]. Generalisability uncertainty refers to the degree to which the results obtained from current clinical trials or economic models can be applied to populations with distinct characteristics specific to the HTA jurisdiction [ , , ]. The characterisation of generalisability uncertainty has not reached consensus in guidelines among HTA jurisdictions [ – ] and in recent frameworks [ , , , ], potentially as it may be addressed through the choice of parameter values and model structure [ , ]. Structural uncertainty typically refers to the uncertainty associated with the economic model structure [ , – , , , , ]. While there is currently no standard definition of structural uncertainty [ ], it generally encompasses any uncertainty that arises from assumptions made about the underlying model, such as model structure or the functional form of relationships between variables [ , ]. The distinction between parameter and structural uncertainty may be considered somewhat artificial given that structural choices could be parameterised, although sometimes with considerable effort [ , ]. Parameter uncertainty arises from a lack of precise information about the “true value” of a parameter [ , – ]. Parameter uncertainty can arise due to missing data, poor quality data, and biased study estimates [ ]. Among these, methodological and structural uncertainty can be further categorised into unparameterisable and parameterisable uncertainty, depending on whether their influences on the ICER can be explored using alternative data inputs, sources or scenarios [ , ]. There is also an inherent hierarchy among the four types of uncertainty, reflecting the sequence of conceptualisation in the modelling (e.g., identifying the place of therapy, comparator and patient population, followed by designing the model structure) and when each type is considered in the decision-making process. The methodological uncertainty would be the first in this sequence and the most important, followed by generalisability, structural, and parameter uncertainty [ , ]. In Australia, the Pharmaceutical Benefits Advisory Committee (PBAC) recommends which medicines should be listed on the Pharmaceutical Benefits Scheme (PBS) and thus receive public funding. The PBAC guidelines list the key factors influencing their decision-making. These key factors include five quantitative factors (i.e., comparative health gain, comparative cost-effectiveness, patient affordability in the absence of PBS subsidy, predicted use in practice and financial implications for the PBS, and predicted use in practice and financial implications for the Australian Government health budget), and other less-readily quantifiable factors (e.g., severity of disease). While the PBAC provides no clear framework for characterising uncertainty, the PBAC and related literature state that the uncertainty around evidence and assumptions in submissions have influenced the funding recommendations [ , – ]. The applicability of existing frameworks for characterising uncertainty in economic models [ , – ] is, to some extent, limited in Australian practice. First, PBAC guidelines did not include a reference

PBS subsidy, predicted use in practice and financial implications for the PBS, and predicted use in practice and financial implications for the Australian Government health budget), and other less-readily quantifiable factors (e.g., severity of disease). While the PBAC provides no clear framework for characterising uncertainty, the PBAC and related literature state that the uncertainty around evidence and assumptions in submissions have influenced the funding recommendations [ , – ]. The applicability of existing frameworks for characterising uncertainty in economic models [ , – ] is, to some extent, limited in Australian practice. First, PBAC guidelines did not include a reference case like other HTA guidelines [e.g., the guidelines of the National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE, England) [ ] and the Canadian Agency for Drugs and Technologies in Health (CADTH, Canada) [ ]]. In theory, methodological uncertainty can be explored by comparing the results of a reference case analysis with those of a non-reference case analysis to examine the influence of methodological differences on the ICER [ ]. The absence of a clearly defined reference case may result in insufficient exploration of methodological uncertainty in Australia. Second, the existing frameworks for characterising uncertainty differ from the categorisation in the PBAC guidelines (i.e., structural, parameter, and translational uncertainty) [ ], posing a challenge to the practical application of existing frameworks. Particularly, the PBAC provide limited procedural guidance on how to systematically characterise structural uncertainty [ ]. Third, the PBAC guidelines do not include some contemporary economic evaluation techniques [ ]. For example, the PBAC only mandates deterministic sensitivity analyses for assessing uncertainty, rather than using probabilistic sensitivity analyses [ ]. This introduces challenges in discerning between uncertainties that can be parameterised with those that cannot, given the key drivers of the economic model are not consistently parameterised. For instance, although the PBAC specifically expresses concerns about generalisability uncertainty and assesses the applicability of the presented evidence to the Australian setting in both clinical and economic evaluations (refer to Sections and A.3 of the PBAC guidelines), sensitivity analysis of the impact of this uncertainty on the ICER was limited in practice. Previous studies have focused on assessing specific sources of uncertainty, such as time horizon, model structure, utility and cost estimation, in the decision-making processes of the pan-Canadian Oncology Drug Review (pCODR), National Health Care Institute (Zorginstituut Nederland, the Netherlands), NICE, and the PBAC [ , – ]. These analyses were typically descriptive and univariate, except for two studies. Harris et al. (2008) analysed 103 PBAC submissions using a probit regression model and found little impact of uncertainty around economic model validity, modelled outcome, and modelled cost on PBAC recommendations [ ]. Harris et al. (2016) extended that study by considering more concrete measures of the uncertainty around economic model validity and modelled outcomes, which significantly influenced the PBAC recommendations [ ]. The evidence being inconclusive in this literature is likely due to the measure of uncertainty being heterogeneous and unsystematic. These two issues are interrelated as defining and measuring uncertainty in HTA decisions has been challenging without a standard framework of classification supported by practical guidelines. Ghabri et al. (2016) is the only empirical study that systematically considered (even though descriptively) different types of uncertainty including methodological, parameter, and structural uncertainty [ ]. Based on 28 submissions, they found that the Haute Autorité de Santé (HAS) in France was most concerned with methodological and parameter uncertainty in their decision-making process and much less with structural uncertainty. The development of a framework to characterise different types of uncertainty in line with the PBAC practice and empirically exploring how these uncertainties influence funding recommendations are needed, as it can help the PBAC better evaluate the robustness of the ICER and thus reduce the probability of incorrect recommendations. It can also help assess if the current evidence is adequate to reduce uncertainty and the value of additional data acquisition [ , ]. In the meantime, such evidence would be valuable to the sponsors, usually pharmaceutical companies, as it can be used to improve their model quality. In this study, we aimed to fill the gaps by developing a standard framework and a practical guideline to characterise different types of uncertainty in economic model-based submissions to the PBAC in Australia. We also empirically assessed their associations with funding recommendations based on a sample of first submissions to the PBAC. In this regard, our primary hypothesis to be tested is that the PBAC was more concerned with the uncertainties placed in the higher levels of hierarchy (e.g., methodological, generalisability, and structural uncertainty) and those that cannot be parameterised based on the available information [ , ]. Methods Development of a Framework for Uncertainty Characterisation A stepwise approach was adopted to develop a framework for characterising the different types of uncertainty in the model-based submissions

model-based submissions to the PBAC in Australia. We also empirically assessed their associations with funding recommendations based on a sample of first submissions to the PBAC. In this regard, our primary hypothesis to be tested is that the PBAC was more concerned with the uncertainties placed in the higher levels of hierarchy (e.g., methodological, generalisability, and structural uncertainty) and those that cannot be parameterised based on the available information [ , ]. Methods Development of a Framework for Uncertainty Characterisation A stepwise approach was adopted to develop a framework for characterising the different types of uncertainty in the model-based submissions to the PBAC. The first step was to establish four types of uncertainty based on the classical textbook [ ] and papers [ , , ]. The second step was to identify all sources of uncertainty from the literature and the PBAC guidelines [ ]. The third step was to allocate these sources of uncertainty into four categories based on the PBAC guidelines and the evaluation practices of the PBAC. We note that it is not our intention to reconcile the differences in the literature regarding how to allocate different sources of uncertainty in general. Rather, our framework intends to reflect the PBAC guidelines and the evaluation practices of the PBAC so that the empirical assessment using the PBAC data could be undertaken more consistently. It is therefore important to note that our framework may not be directly used in other contexts. The framework is illustrated in Fig. . It is worth noting that methodological and structural uncertainty were further subcategorised into parameterisable and unparameterisable uncertainty based on the value of information theory [ , ]. Each type of uncertainty is formally defined below, and details on related PBAC judgments are presented in Appendix in the electronic supplementary material (ESM). Methodological uncertainty was defined as the deviations from the PBAC guidelines, in the absence of a reference case. As shown in the top section of Figure , unparameterisable methodological uncertainty arose when the proposed clinical management algorithms and proposed PBS listing were not consistent with current clinical practice in Australia, the submission nominated the wrong comparator(s), or a broader or narrower (than the healthcare system) perspective of the economic evaluation was adopted. Parameterisable methodological uncertainty arose if the cost or outcomes were not discounted uniformly at an annual rate of 5%, or if the utility was estimated from external sources rather than pivotal clinical trials, or if the scoring algorithm of the instrument to elicit utility was not derived from the general population in Australia. Generalisability uncertainty was defined as when the characteristics of participants of the clinical trials or the modelled population were not representative of the target (i.e., PBS) population. It is noteworthy that generalisability uncertainty pertained specifically to the concerns the PBAC expressed regarding the applicability to the PBS population without consideration of whether it could be explored using alternative data sources (e.g., intention-to-treat population or subgroup population). If the sponsor used evidence based on a subgroup population to explore generalisability uncertainty, the correspondent parameter uncertainty was considered negligible. By doing so, generalisability uncertainty would have captured the downstream uncertainty (i.e., parameter uncertainty). Unparameterisable structural uncertainty arose when the model conceptualisation was flawed (such as the set-up of the health states and the direction of transition of patients between health states). Parameterisable structural uncertainty was specific to extrapolation uncertainty and occurred when any of the assumptions considered were uncertain when choosing the time horizon, time dependency on transition probabilities, treatment duration or the parametric survival model. Parameter uncertainty was defined as uncertainty around the estimation of the clinical effectiveness (or transition possibilities), utility or cost. Such uncertainty arose from inappropriate assumptions, data limitations or poor quality of evidence. Data collection Sample identification The medicine-indication pairs were identified from the Public Summary Documents (PSDs), which provide information regarding the health and economic evidence considered and the rationale of the PBAC judgement regarding whether to recommend a medicine for public funding. The PSDs based on the first major submission of the eligible medicines and vaccines were included if they were released between 2014 and 2021 and presented a cost-utility analysis. The year 2014 was chosen as the starting point because it was the first time that the PSDs included more detailed information on the target population, comparators and economic benefits [ ]. Only the first submission of a medicine–indication pair was included, as it reflects the unbiased behaviour of sponsors without being influenced by the restrictions or lower price requirements from HTA bodies (i.e., the PBAC) [ ], and the first submission was more comprehensive in terms of the evidence considered and uncertainties present. Only the first submission of a medicine–indication pair was included, as it reflects the unbiased behaviour of sponsors without being influenced by the restrictions or lower price requirements from HTA bodies (i.e., the PBAC) [ ], and the first submission was more comprehensive in terms of the evidence considered and uncertainties present. The samples of PSDs were considered multiple times when the sponsor proposed multiple indications based on different economic models or constructed different models for the nominated comparators for one indication (see Appendix in ESM for detailed inclusion/exclusion criteria of PSDs). Data extraction A practical guide was developed to extract information regarding whether the medicine (vaccine)–indication pair was recommended, whether the PBAC raised a concern with a certain type of uncertainty, and the other relevant factors that could influence the PBAC recommendations (see Appendix in ESM for detailed information regarding data extracted). When the submission did not report the PBAC’s view, we considered the view of the Economics Sub-Committee who critically assessed the submissions with a focus on the economic evaluation components. Data extraction was conducted by the first author (Q.F.) and cross-checked by research assistants. Cohen’s kappa value was used to assess the inter-rater reliability of reviewers (see Appendix in ESM). A random 5% sample was also checked by a senior co-author (V.J.). No major individual bias was identified. Statistical Analysis A descriptive analysis of the uncertainties from submissions was first conducted, following the practice in the previous literature. We calculated the frequency of each uncertainty source and the resulting frequency of each type of uncertainty based on our categorisation. It is worth noting that one uncertainty type occurred as long as one of the sources under it was identified. Univariate analysis was undertaken to assess whether each source of uncertainty was associated with the funding recommendations. Our main analysis was based on the multivariate logistic regression model where different types of uncertainty were considered simultaneously, with other relevant factors being controlled, including the safety profile, the statistical significance of clinical effectiveness, financial implications on PBS, the severity of disease and the base case ICER [ , – , , ]. These control variables were selected based on the PBAC guidelines, which listed key factors influencing their decision-making. The justification and the measurement of control variables are documented in Appendix in the ESM. To alleviate any concern of multicollinearity and conceptually overlapping among different sources of uncertainty, Kendall’s tau-b coefficient and its p value were used to measure the potential correlations between different types (and sources) of uncertainty. To quantify the size of the effect, we calculated the average marginal effects (AME) of each uncertainty on the probability of a positive funding recommendation [ ]. A p value less than 0.05 was taken as the evidence of significant associations and all statistical analyses were conducted using STATA 17. To ensure the validity of the results, we conducted several robustness checks, including (1) using additional control variables in the regression analysis (i.e., PBAC’s concerns on clinical magnitude and unmet clinical need), (2) measuring parameterisable structural uncertainty using three levels (low, medium, high), (3) measuring parameter uncertainty using three variables: uncertainty around cost, utility, and clinical effectiveness (or transition possibilities), (4) using a probit model, (5) remeasuring generalisability uncertainty to focus only on unparameterisable generalisability, (6) interacting the statistical significance of clinical benefit and parameter uncertainty, and (7) pooling parameterisable methodological uncertainty and parameter uncertainty around utility to test whether the uncertainty around utility was not associated with the PBAC recommendations [ ]. In the logistic regression, the functional form of the independent variables was assumed to be linear additive. It is certainly possible that they may have impacted the decision interactively. However, due to the limited sample size, it was unrealistic to introduce multiple interactions in the regression analyses. Instead, following Charokopou et al. (2015) [ ] and Karikios et al. (2017) [ ], we used the classification and regression trees (CART) approach to investigate how different sources of uncertainty impacted the decision interactively and sequentially. CART is a non-parametric statistical technique used to construct a binary decision tree. It is suitable for identifying significant patterns among the independent variables (i.e., sources of uncertainty) to help predict a binary dependent variable (i.e., positive or negative recommendations). CART has advantages over the logistic regression model to handle complex relationships, but it cannot provide a marginal contribution to the overall probability of a positive recommendation for each variable. Results Basic Statistics of Uncertainty Our analysis included 193 medicine–indication pairs for their first submission, consisting of 184 medicine–indication pairs and 9 vaccines. The flowchart outlining the inclusion process is presented in Appendix in ESM. Descriptive statistics of the medicine–indication pairs are included in Table . The most common type of medicines included in the submissions was cancer medicines (112, 58%), followed by medicines for the treatment of other chronic diseases (52, 27%) and rare diseases (20, 10%). A total of 153 (79%) submissions were rejected or deferred upon initial submission, with rejection rates of 84% for cancer medicines and 80% for orphan drugs. Table provides an overview of the prevalence of uncertainties identified in the included medicine–indication pairs by uncertainty type and sources. Overall, parameter uncertainty was the predominant type mentioned by the PBAC (184, 95%) even though the related sources (clinical effectiveness, utility, and cost) were not significantly associated with the probability of recommendations. The second most mentioned type was parameterisable structural uncertainty (161, 83%). Sources of parameterisable structural uncertainty pertained to extrapolation issues, encompassing an inappropriate time horizon (106, 55%), an unjustified relationship between time and transition possibilities or treatment effect (97, 50%), and uncertainty in the choice of parametric survival model (92, 48%), which were all significantly associated with an increased probability of recommendations (marginal effects: 0.167–0.230). Sources of unparameterisable structural uncertainty mainly stemmed from unjustified assumptions about the transition of patients between health states (57, 30%), among which only the uncertain relationship between surrogate outcome and the clinical endpoint was found to have a significant association with the probability of recommendations (marginal effect: 0.152). The third most common type was unparameterisable methodological uncertainty (108, 56%). The most common source of unparameterisable methodological uncertainty was the inconsistency with the clinical place in therapy or the proposed PBS restriction (84, 44%), which had a significant association with the probability of recommendations (marginal effect: 0.283). Parameterisable methodological uncertainty was mainly related to valuing health gains, particularly when submissions did not obtain their utility values from clinical trials (81, 42%) or did not use scoring algorithms based on the general population in Australia (32, 17%). However, only the latter was statistically significant (marginal effect: 0.136). Finally, a total of 93 (48%) submissions were considered to have generalisability uncertainty which had a statistically significant association with the probability of recommendations (marginal effect: 0.213). Logistic Regression Analysis Given the systematic approach adopted for the variable definitions and data extractions, strong correlations among different types of uncertainty are unlikely. Nevertheless, Kendall’s tau-b coefficients showed that they are indeed very weakly or weakly correlated (see Appendix in ESM). Table presents the logistic regression parameter estimates (column 2) and the AME estimates for each independent variable (column 3). While the signs of the coefficients were all as expected, only three out of the six types of uncertainty had a statistically significant effect on the funding recommendations. The logistic regression results suggested that the PBAC was more likely to recommend a medicine by 15.0%, 10.2 %, and 17.6%, respectively, when unparameterisable methodological, generalisability or parameterisable structural uncertainty was eliminated. By contrast, parameterisable methodological uncertainty and unparameterisable structural uncertainty did not have a significant association with the probability of positive recommendations. The lack of a significant association was also found for parameter uncertainty, albeit being the most common type of uncertainty (see Table ). Among the control variables, the clinical effectiveness, superior or non-inferior safety profile and base case ICER lower than A$45,000/QALY were statistically significantly associated with the probability of positive recommendations. This is somewhat expected since these three control variables were primary factors the PBAC considered in their decision-making process in the guidelines [ ]. The results from the robustness check were overall consistent with those reported here (see Appendix in ESM). The result of the CART analysis echoed the main result of the logistic analysis. It suggested that the sources of uncertainty with the greatest discriminative power for PBAC recommendation were: (1) inconsistency between the proposed treatment and either its clinical place in therapy or the restriction listed on the PBS schedule (i.e., one source of unparameterisable methodological uncertainty), (2) an unjustified relationship between time and transition probabilities or treatment effect, (3) generalisability uncertainty, and (4) uncertainty around the parametric survival model. The second and the last ones were sources of parameterisable structural uncertainty (i.e., extrapolation) (see Appendix in ESM). The second and the last ones were sources of parameterisable structural uncertainty (i.e., extrapolation) (see Appendix in ESM). Discussion and Limitations To the best of our knowledge, this study is the first to develop a holistic framework encompassing the different types of uncertainty that may be associated with the PBAC recommendations. This framework was built on the previous work [ , – ], but was more aligned with PBAC guidelines and the practices of the PBAC. For example, rather than categorising all the sources of uncertainty around utility as parameter uncertainty, we categorised them as two types of uncertainty: parameterisable methodological uncertainty and parameter uncertainty. The former represents the case when trial-based utility and Australian population-based utility scoring algorithms were not used in a submission. Another example is an inappropriate time horizon, the PBAC guideline regards it as one source of structural uncertainty [ ], while the framework proposed by Bilcke et al. (2011) considered it as one source of methodological uncertainty [ ]. Furthermore, this study subcategorised uncertainty as parameterisable and unparameterisable uncertainty based on whether the information could be available in the near future. By doing so, the uncertainty could be distinguished as the part that could be mitigated and those that cannot at the time of submission. Unlike previous studies that had not comprehensively measured the uncertainty around the economic model, we focused on the characterisation of different types of uncertainty and their association with PBAC recommendations. Although the characterisation of uncertainties in Harris et al. (2008, 2016) differed from our framework [ , ] and their medicines (the submissions from 1993 to 2009) differed from our sample, it is evident that the PBAC’s concerns regarding uncertainty have evolved, particularly regarding the economic evaluation. From 1994 to 2004, Harris et al. (2008) found the effect of structural uncertainty was underrepresented due to the dominance of clinical effectiveness considerations by the PBAC [ ]. However, they found it became significant in 2009 [ ]. Based on the analysis of submissions from 2014 to 2021, our study found that the PBAC mainly focused on parameterisable structural uncertainty, unparameterisable methodological uncertainty and generalisability uncertainty. Despite not being based on the same medicine–indication pairs, our results revealed that some uncertainties raised by the PBAC were also emphasised by the pCODR and HAS, such as the choice of comparators, specification of data sources, and time horizon [ , ]. Although the PBAC does not acknowledge an explicit ICER threshold [ ], they explicitly state in the PBAC guidelines that the uncertainty (i.e., overall confidence) around evidence and assumptions relied on submissions influences their recommendations. Their concerns about the uncertainty were reflected by this study. Our study conceptually characterised uncertainty raised by the PBAC into the hierarchy of methodological, generalisability, structural, and parameter uncertainty (methodological and structural uncertainty were further subcategorised into parameterisable and unparameterisable uncertainty). In line with the level of uncertainty in economic evaluation of HTA proposed by Grutters et al. (2015) [ ] and Briggs et al. (2000) [ ], our empirical results reflected this inherent hierarchy. As demonstrated in Fig. , we found that first submissions of included medicine–indication pairs without unparameterisable methodological, generalisability, and parameterisable structural uncertainty were more likely to be recommended by the PBAC. Unparameterisable methodological uncertainty cannot be regarded as a real uncertainty but rather an early-stage issue in economic evaluation [ ], as it is highly related to the reference case specific to the decision context [ ]. Without proper formalisation of the decision problem, the subsequent process of comparator(s) selection, data collection, evidence synthesis and analytic model construction could be misguided [ ]. We found a 15.0% (95% CI 6.1–24.0%) increase in the probability of a positive recommendation for medicines without such uncertainty, which underscores the importance of formalising the decision problem aligned with the Australian context by scrutinising the treatment guidelines of the target disease and then proposing acceptable PBS restrictions before submission. Our study also included alignment of the Therapeutic Goods Administration (TGA, the regulator in Australia) and the PBAC regarding the proposed indication or clinical place as one source of this type of uncertainty. The findings also suggest that sponsors need to carefully choose when to submit their medicines to the PBAC and strictly adhere to the TGA-approved indication. the Australian context by scrutinising the treatment guidelines of the target disease and then proposing acceptable PBS restrictions before submission. Our study also included alignment of the Therapeutic Goods Administration (TGA, the regulator in Australia) and the PBAC regarding the proposed indication or clinical place as one source of this type of uncertainty. The findings also suggest that sponsors need to carefully choose when to submit their medicines to the PBAC and strictly adhere to the TGA-approved indication. This finding was further confirmed by the additional results of CART analysis (see Appendix in ESM), which demonstrated that “the proposed clinical management algorithms and proposed PBS listing were not consistent with current clinical practice in Australia” was the primary discriminative factor. The PBAC particularly requires sponsors to describe the demographic and patient characteristics in the clinical trial(s) and the economic model, translating the important applicability concerns to the Australian context. These concerns were reflected by the significant association between generalisability uncertainty and the positive funding recommendations in this study. However, it remains unclear whether generating Australia-specific evidence is worthwhile given the costs of generating such evidence. Regarding structural uncertainty, the latest PBAC guidelines highlight structural uncertainty related to the parameterisable (i.e. extrapolation) and unparameterisable (i.e. model structure) uncertainty [ , ]. In terms of parameterisable structural uncertainty (i.e. extrapolation), our study confirmed that the PBAC strongly adhered to the guidelines, with the largest influence [17.6 % (95% CI 5.6–29.7%)] on positive recommendations for medicines without this structural uncertainty. This result also echoed the quantitative survey conducted by Kim et al. (2022), which found that respondents from academia, government, and industry in Australia had divided opinions on the extrapolation of survival data [ ]. This reflected the PBAC’s concern about the causal relationship between treatments and long-term patient-relevant endpoints. As more medicines with new mechanisms of action are approved by regulators (e.g. the TGA in Australia) based on immature clinical data (i.e., early phase of clinical trials or uncertain surrogate outcome) [ – ], extrapolation has become a common challenge for HTA bodies due to several methodological challenges [ ]. The methodological challenges may arise from limited knowledge available to both sponsors and HTA bodies at the time of submission, impeding efforts to mitigate structural uncertainty (e.g., model structure, patients’ transition, and the relationship between surrogate outcomes and clinical endpoints). In terms of unparameterisable structural uncertainty (i.e., model structure), the PBAC prefers a formal approach to quantify the impacts of different structures when there is sufficient clinical evidence or expert opinion available. However, the choice of approach to address structural uncertainty depends on the preferences of appraisal committees (e.g., acceptance of expert opinion, quantitative or qualitative approaches to judging the potential impact of alternative plausible assumptions on model predictions), which have not reached a consensus [ ]. Unexpectedly, our study did not find a significant association between unparameterisable structural uncertainty and recommendations. As depicted in Fig. , instead of simply interpreting this result as the PBAC ignoring uncertainty around model structure, it is better interpreted as the PBAC acknowledging that it was a source of uncertainty, but there may not be alternative model structure(s) that can adequately capture the relevant disease characteristics and proposed treatments due to available knowledge [ ]. This is particularly prevalent in rare diseases, where sponsors constructed different model structures for the same medicine–indication pairs. For example, in the submission of amifampridine [ ], an orphan medicine for the treatment of Lambert–Eaton myasthenic syndrome in adults and children aged 6 years, the definition of health states was different between the PBAC and CADTH (Canada) submissions. The submission defined health states according to the responder rate in the PBAC submission, while submission to CADTH was based on the severity of Quantitative Myasthenia Gravis scores. These differences partially explain why the ICER presented to the PBAC was almost one-third of the estimate presented to CADTH. Aligning with expectations, parameterisable methodological and parameter uncertainty were not significantly associated with positive recommendations. However, interpreting the following results should be done with caution. First, the non-significant association between the discount rate (i.e., one source of parameterisable methodological uncertainty) and the PBAC recommendations cannot be easily interpreted as a lack of concern by the PBAC regarding adherence to the required 5% discount rate for health benefits and costs. Although different discount rates were used by sponsors in only six submissions, which resulted in insufficient statistical power to reach a conclusion, the homogeneous rejected recommendations and comments in the PSDs could reflect the PBAC response to this issue. This was in line with the PBAC’s feedback to relevant stakeholders regarding the changing of the discount rate for Australian HTA [ ]. Second, the association between parameter uncertainty and the PBAC recommendation also faced a similar issue of low statistical power. Due to our measurement of

PBAC regarding adherence to the required 5% discount rate for health benefits and costs. Although different discount rates were used by sponsors in only six submissions, which resulted in insufficient statistical power to reach a conclusion, the homogeneous rejected recommendations and comments in the PSDs could reflect the PBAC response to this issue. This was in line with the PBAC’s feedback to relevant stakeholders regarding the changing of the discount rate for Australian HTA [ ]. Second, the association between parameter uncertainty and the PBAC recommendation also faced a similar issue of low statistical power. Due to our measurement of parameter uncertainty which pooled the uncertainty around cost, utility and clinical effectiveness (or transition probabilities) in one variable, there were only nine medicine pairs that did not have parameter uncertainty. Consequently, it is not surprising that we failed to detect a statistically significant influence of parameter uncertainty on recommendations. Following Harris et al. (2008) [ ], we took an additional step to estimate the influence of individual sources of parameter uncertainty on the PBAC recommendations. Both the results of the robustness check and univariate analysis were in line with the findings in the main model, showing uncertainty around clinical effectiveness (or transition probabilities), utility and cost individually did not have a significant association with the PBAC positive recommendations. Third, although we exclude the potential correlation between uncertainty around how to value health gains (i.e., one source of parameterisable methodological uncertainty) and parameter uncertainty around utility values, this did not help to observe the association between PBAC’s specific methodological concerns regarding how to value health gains and PBAC recommendations. We further pooled these two sources of uncertainty into parameters around utility in robustness check (see Model 7 in Appendix of ESM) but did not find a significant association between uncertainty around utility and the PBAC recommendations. These additional results increase our confidence in suggesting that the PBAC tended to be less concerned about parameter uncertainty in the first submission, as their impact on the ICER can be quantified, and thus the associated risk of making a wrong decision can be easily quantified by using alternative data inputs, sources, or scenarios in subsequent submissions. Our study has important policy implications for both sponsors and the PBAC to manage the uncertainty. First, sponsors and the PBAC need to increase early dialogue regarding which uncertainties are considered relevant and what their potential consequences are. This would encourage them to acknowledge the necessity of additional information about uncertainty [ ]. For those sources of uncertainty with significant consequences, it is essential to distinguish between uncertainties that can be resolved with current evidence or additional evidence that can be gathered at reasonable cost, and those that cannot be addressed in the short term. This approach would enable the identification of situations where managed entry agreements to collect more data are valuable versus negotiating prices to reduce uncertainty [ ]. Second, when the influence of structural uncertainty, including parameterisable and unparameterisable parts, is unavoidable based on current evidence and cannot be mitigated by good modelling practice, disease-specific or medicine class-specific model standards (or multi-use models) should be developed that reflect specific treatment algorithms, extrapolation (e.g. disease progression, assumption of treatment effect and time horizon) and treatment-specific utilities [ ]. Lastly, early collaboration between the PBAC and the sponsors is necessary to formalise decision problems in the context of Australia, as uncertainty around unparameterisable methodological and generalisability are heavily dependent on Australian clinical practice and PBS restriction requirements, which cannot be accounted for in a one-size-fits-all reference case. An efficient pre-submission meeting involving sponsors with HTA bodies is one potential solution. Pre-submissions in the application process are in place in the UK and Canada. NICE arranges early scoping meetings to discuss decision problems, including the identification of the most likely comparator(s) and appropriate endpoints to estimate the cost-effectiveness of proposed medicines [ ]. Despite there being no comparable process to the NICE scientific consultation during pre-submission [ ], pCODR in Canada also performs a pre-submission process to promote early communication on the approach to the clinical and economic evaluation and a better understanding of the potential needs for the CADTH [ , ]. The PBAC has started to improve an open dialogue with submitters by introducing a two-stage PBS process that commenced in July 2019 [ ]. One task of this process improvement is to change pre‐submission meetings and to improve guidance and support and submission quality for complex submissions, regarding providing clarity around the evidence and the data required [ , ]. While it is too early to assess the influence of these improvements due to the short implementation time, this study found that unparameterisable methodological uncertainty was likely to undermine the confidence of the PBAC recommendation, and hence the two-stage PBS process is promising. A formal patient/population, intervention, comparison and outcomes (PICO) assessment is another strategy. A formal PICO assessment before an evaluation has already been adopted by other HTA bodies. For instance, the Medical Services Advisory Committee (MSAC), an HTA body in Australia which is responsible for appraising new non-drug health technologies, has a PICO advisory sub-committee to clearly articulate each element of the PICO, and the decision analytic framework for preparing the subsequent economic evaluation [ , ]. The European Network for HTA has also established a “PICO working group” to define guiding principles [ – ]. This study has some limitations. First, it only provides an overview of the association between the PBAC recommendations and the four types of uncertainty. The influence of uncertainty in specific medicine-indication pairs (i.e., cancer or rare disease) needs to be explored individually. Second, this study only included the first submission of medicine-indication pairs without considering any subsequent resubmissions, which reduced the sample and limited the exploration of whether one type of uncertainty interacts with other uncertainties. Resubmissions of medicine will provide directions for future research to investigate how sponsors address uncertainties in response to PBAC concerns after the first rejection.Third, our findings heavily relied on what was explicitly reported in the PSDs. Additional discussions about uncertainties may have taken place during PBAC committee meetings, however, this remains unclear due to the unavailability of publicly accessible meeting minutes and the submissions made by the sponsors. Conclusion This study formally characterised the uncertainty around the model-based submissions to the PBAC based on the first submissions for medicine–indication pairs, as well as explored their association with funding recommendations. To improve the model quality and the probability of positive recommendation, both the PBAC and sponsors should focus on reducing unparameterisable methodological, generalisability and parameterisable structural uncertainty. Several policy implications were provided, including the systematic characterisation of uncertainties that can help distinguish between those that can be resolved with additional evidence that can be gathered at a reasonable cost, and those inherent in the disease or treatment that cannot be addressed in the short term and may need to be accepted; early collaboration between both stakeholders is needed to formalise decision problems in the context of Australia and reduce methodological uncertainty and more disease-specific model standards (or multi-use models) can also help mitigate structural uncertainty.
